title: When the student cannot answer the question
author: Doan Winkel
source: howtoteachwithai.substack.com (How to Teach With AI), September 28, 2026
summary: Doan Winkel follows up on his earlier "checkpoint" routine of asking every student three questions about each assignment, by addressing the hardest moment: the student who cannot explain a choice in their own paper. His advice is to resist filling the silence with an explanation, because that is where an accusation leaks in, and to avoid asking whether the student used AI, since the answer is either an undetectable lie or an admission the teacher must then process. Instead he asks a second question about what the student wanted the paper to say that it does not yet say, then gives a short, no-penalty rewrite deadline of three days. He closes by redesigning the assignment itself so students must record one decision made and one rejected in under three minutes, moving the grade to the part a chatbot cannot produce.
points: Do not fill the silence or explain why you asked, because the explanation is where the accusation leaks into the conversation.
Avoid asking whether the student used AI; ask instead what they wanted the paper to say that it does not say yet, a question they can answer however the draft was written.
A short, no-penalty rewrite deadline (three days) removes the incentive to lie and spreads the expectation through the class by word of mouth.
Fix the assignment, not just the conversation: require a brief recorded account of one decision made and one rejected, and weight it above polish.
Pick one upcoming assignment and spend ten minutes redesigning it rather than overhauling the entire course.
quotes: The instinct is to explain why I asked. I have to resist it. The explanation is where the accusation leaks in, and once it leaks I’m in a process neither of us wanted.

Don’t ask whether they used AI. The answer is either a lie I can’t disprove or an admission I now have to report, and both are worse than the thing I actually want, which is a better paper written by this student.
They can answer that one no matter how the draft got written. It moves the conversation off what they did and onto what they still owe me.
A student who leaned on AI usually has a real answer ready, because they already know the paper is thin. Nobody had ever asked.
Three days is short enough to keep this about the paragraph and long enough that nobody can claim there was no time. No penalty removes the only reason left to lie about it.
By Friday some part of that class knows you ask about paragraphs and that the rewrite is free. Every paper after that gets written by somebody who assumes a question is coming.
That moves the grade onto the only part a chatbot cannot produce: the record of a choice made by a person who had options.
The hallway conversation takes three minutes. The rewrite takes ten. Skipping both is also a decision, and it is the one that shows up in every paper you grade for the rest of the term.
